children: Gold and silver have firmly reclaimed their positions as the global economy’s primary insurance policy. Driven by geopolitical conflicts, global trade friction, and unpredictable interest rate cycles, both precious metals surged to historic highs in 2025. Annual global gold demand climbed toward 5,000 tonnes, while silver demand exceeded mine supply for a fifth consecutive year. Yet beyond the record-breaking prices lie three fundamental structural shifts redefining the market landscape.

First, global demand has undergone a structural pivot: financial investors have overtaken traditional jewellers as the primary drivers of gold buying. Surging Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF) inflows, robust physical bar purchases, and continuous central bank buying have established a strong structural floor under the market. Second, silver has evolved into a true hybrid asset: part traditional haven, part essential industrial commodity required for solar photovoltaics, electric vehicles, and AI infrastructure. Because silver is largely mined as a byproduct of other metals, its supply cannot easily scale up to meet this industrial demand.

The third and most transformative shift is unfolding within India. The nation is transitioning from wearing gold to owning it as a strategic investment. Indian bar and coin demand hit record levels even as discretionary jewellery purchases slowed. Concurrently, domestic commodity exchanges such as the Multi Commodity Exchange of India (MCX) demonstrate deep liquidity, sophisticated risk-management tools, and seamless physical delivery mechanisms. The adoption of Good Delivery Standards, permitting domestically refined gold and silver to settle exchange contracts, marks a crucial milestone in maturing the country’s bullion derivatives ecosystem.
This evolution underpins a broader strategic vision for Indian commodity markets: Price in India, Hedge in India, Invest in India, and Manage Risk in India.

As the world’s most established market, bullion serves as the anchor for India’s emerging commodity framework. The widespread adoption of domestic price benchmarks on exchanges like MCX provides a blueprint for base metals, energy, and agricultural commodities. Rather than relying on overseas exchanges, Indian market participants, SMEs, and institutional investors can discover fair local prices and hedge their exposure within a neutral, secure, and transparent ecosystem. Exchange-traded commodity derivatives (ETCDs) further offer investors an efficient avenue for portfolio diversification.

By establishing robust domestic price references, enforcing zero-tolerance policies against unethical trade practices, and leveraging technology for exceptional trade efficiencies, India is bridging the gap between primary producers and end consumers. As structural shifts elevate gold and silver on the world stage, India’s deepening financial infrastructure ensures its influence in global bullion will finally match its massive stature as a global consumer.

title: Gold, silver, and India’s coming of age as a bullion market
